added_claim_errors: The smallest-of formula is wrong: with $4,000 compensation and $2,000 other IRA contributions, it permits $4,000 instead of $2,000.
“Your 2004 account passes the 15-year test” assumes beneficiary continuity that the request does not establish.
“If the money lands in January ... the 2026 room is lost” overlooks designation for 2026 through April 15, 2027, subject to plan processing.
“If annual limits rise, it could take fewer years” is unsupported by announced limits; even $8,000 annually requires five years.
“The 529 plan probably will not verify his income or other contributions” is an unsupported prediction about the unidentified plan.
The smallest-of formula and instruction to subtract other contributions from $7,500 are wrong when compensation is lower: $4,000 compensation minus $2,000 contributions leaves $2,000, not $4,000.

reasons: B wins because it corrects the December deadline, explains both tax consequences of an excessive transfer, and covers the income-phase-out exception that A omits. Both immediately reject the $48,000 premise, but both give an unsafe annual-limit formula when compensation is below $7,500 and other IRA contributions exist. B still omits the $40,500 calculation, the corrective-withdrawal deadline, and explicit confirmation that prior-year processing and coding vary by plan; A adds misleading deadline and timeline claims. Both are unnecessarily long and repetitive. I opened the [IRS Form 1099-Q instructions](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1099q), which confirm B’s added Box 4b reporting detail.
